seoDescription: Learn to structure your ASP.NET Core applications for maintainability by creating a dedicated service to handle data retrieval. This guide walks through the entire process, explaining the single responsibility principle and how to implement it. You'll see how to create a `JsonFileProductService` to read data from a JSON file, leverage the `IWebHostEnvironment` to reliably locate files, and use `System.Text.Json` to deserialize data into C# objects.

chapters.title: Introduction to Services
chapters.description: This chapter explains the importance of services for maintainability and introduces the single responsibility principle using a restaurant waiter analogy.

chapters.title: Creating the Service Folder and File
chapters.description: This chapter covers creating a dedicated 'services' folder and adding a new C# class file named 'JsonFileProductsService' to house the data logic.

chapters.title: Pasting and Organizing the Service Code
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates pasting in the service code and using Visual Studio's code folding feature to make the complex class more readable.

chapters.title: The Service Constructor and IWebHostEnvironment
chapters.description: This chapter breaks down the service's constructor, explaining how it uses dependency injection to receive an IWebHostEnvironment instance.

chapters.title: Constructing the JSON File Path
chapters.description: This chapter explains how to use Path.Combine with the WebRootPath to reliably build the file path to the JSON data, avoiding hardcoded paths.

chapters.title: Deserializing JSON Data with GetProducts
chapters.description: This chapter examines the GetProducts method, showing how it uses JsonSerializer to deserialize the JSON file into an enumerable collection of Product objects.

chapters.title: Registering the Service in Startup.cs
chapters.description: This chapter explains how to register the new service with ASP.NET Core's dependency injection container within the ConfigureServices method in Startup.cs.

chapters.title: Conclusion and Next Steps
chapters.description: This chapter concludes by running the application to confirm it works and explaining why this foundational work is crucial before displaying data.

summary:
## Why Use a Service?

A service is a component that performs a specific task for other parts of the application. Using services helps create more maintainable and reusable code.

- **Single Responsibility Principle**: Each part of the application should have only one job. The service's job is to retrieve product data, separating that concern from the web page that displays it.
- **Maintainability**: If the data source changes (e.g., from a JSON file to a database), you only need to update the service, not every page that uses the data.
- **Reusability**: Other parts of the application can easily use the same service to get product data.

> [!NOTE]
> A service is like a waiter in a restaurant: you ask for what you need, and the waiter gets it for you without you needing to know how the kitchen works.

## Creating the `JsonFileProductService`

1.  **Create a `services` folder** in the root of the project to organize your service classes.
2.  **Add a new C# class file** named `JsonFileProductService.cs` inside the a `services` folder.

## Understanding the Service Code

The `JsonFileProductService` class is responsible for reading and parsing the `products.json` file.

### The Constructor and `IWebHostEnvironment`

The constructor receives an `IWebHostEnvironment` object via **dependency injection**. ASP.NET automatically provides this service.

```csharp
public JsonFileProductService(IWebHostEnvironment webHostEnvironment)
{
    WebHostEnvironment = webHostEnvironment;
}
```

This is used to get reliable information about the web application's hosting environment, such as file paths.

### Building the File Path

To avoid hardcoding file paths (e.g., `C:\...`), the service builds the path dynamically.

- **`WebHostEnvironment.WebRootPath`**: This property reliably gets the absolute path to the `wwwroot` folder, which is designed to contain public, static assets.
- **`System.IO.Path.Combine()`**: This helper method safely combines path segments, handling path separators (`/` or `\`) correctly for any operating system.

```csharp
private string JsonFileName
{
    get { return Path.Combine(WebHostEnvironment.WebRootPath, "data", "products.json"); }
}
```

### The `GetProducts` Method

This method reads the JSON file, deserializes it into C# objects, and returns them.

- **Deserialization**: It uses `System.Text.Json.JsonSerializer.Deserialize` to convert the JSON text into an array of `Product` objects (`Product[]`).
- **Case Insensitivity**: It passes an option to the deserializer to ignore differences in case between the JSON properties and the C# model properties (`PropertyNameCaseInsensitive = true`).
- **`IEnumerable<Product>`**: The method returns an `IEnumerable<Product>`. This is a flexible, read-only collection interface that allows the caller to iterate over the products without being tied to a specific collection type like a `List` or an `array`.

## Registering the Service (Dependency Injection)

For the rest of the application to be able to use the service, it must be "registered" in the `Startup.cs` file.

- **`ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services)`**: This method in `Startup.cs` is where you configure your application's services.
- **`services.AddTransient<JsonFileProductService>()`**: This line registers the service with the dependency injection (DI) container.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Service Lifetimes**:
> - `AddTransient()`: A new instance of the service is created every time it's requested. This is useful for lightweight, stateless services.
> - `AddSingleton()`: A single instance is created for the entire application's lifetime.
